entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 42
 
Ge 42:1-38. Journey into Egypt.

1. Now when Jacob saw that there was corn in Egypt--learned from common rumor. It is evident from Jacob's language that his own and his sons' families had suffered greatly from the scarcity; and through the increasing severity of the scourge, those men, who had formerly shown both activity and spirit, were sinking into despondency. God would not interpose miraculously when natural means of preservation were within reach.
entries.reader_content_plain:
CHAPTER 42
 
Ge 42:1-38. Journey into Egypt.

1. Now when Jacob saw that there was corn in Egypt--learned from common rumor. It is evident from Jacob's language that his own and his sons' families had suffered greatly from the scarcity; and through the increasing severity of the scourge, those men, who had formerly shown both activity and spirit, were sinking into despondency. God would not interpose miraculously when natural means of preservation were within reach.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv488"/><div sID="gen710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv488"/><hi type="bold">5. the famine was in the land of Canaan--</hi>The tropical rains, which annually falling swell the Nile, are those of Palestine also; and their failure would produce the same disastrous effects in Canaan as in Egypt. Numerous caravans of its people, therefore, poured over the sandy desert of Suez, with their beasts of burden, for the purchase of corn; and among others, "the sons of Israel" were compelled to undertake a journey from which painful associations made them strongly averse. <div eID="gen710" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv490"/><div sID="gen714" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv490"/><hi type="bold">7-8. Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, ... but they knew not him--</hi>This is not strange. They were full-grown men--he was but a lad at parting. They were in their usual garb--he was in his official robes. They never dreamt of him as governor of Egypt, while he had been expecting them. They had but one face; he had ten persons to judge by.<div eID="gen714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly--</hi>It would be an injustice to Joseph's character to suppose that this stern manner was prompted by any vindictive feelings--he never indulged any resentment against others who had injured him. But he spoke in the authoritative tone of the governor in order to elicit some much-longed-for information respecting the state of his father's family, as well as to bring his brethren, by their own humiliation and distress, to a sense of the evils they had done to him. <div eID="gen715" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv491"/><div sID="gen716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv491"/><hi type="bold">9-14. Ye are spies--</hi>This is a suspicion entertained regarding strangers in all Eastern countries down to the present day. Joseph, however, who was well aware that his brethren were not spies, has been charged with cruel dissimulation, with a deliberate violation of what he knew to be the truth, in imputing to them such a character. But it must be remembered that he was sustaining the part of a ruler; and, in fact, acting on the very principle sanctioned by many of the sacred writers, and our Lord Himself, who spoke parables (fictitious stories) to promote a good end. <div eID="gen716" type="x-p"/>

Me have ye bereaved--</hi>This exclamation indicates a painfully excited state of feeling, and it shows how difficult it is for even a good man to yield implicit submission to the course of Providence. The language does not imply that his missing sons had got foul play from the hands of the rest, but he looks upon Simeon as lost, as well as Joseph, and he insinuates it was by some imprudent statements of theirs that he was exposed to the risk of losing Benjamin also. <div eID="gen724" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv499"/><div sID="gen725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv499"/><hi type="bold">37. Reuben spake, ... Slay my two sons, if I bring him not to thee--</hi>This was a thoughtless and unwarrantable condition--one that he never seriously expected his father would accept. It was designed only to give assurance of the greatest care being taken of Benjamin. But unforeseen circumstances might arise to render it impossible for all of them to preserve that young lad (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.13">Jas 4:13</reference>), and Jacob was much pained by the prospect. Little did he know that God was dealing with him severely, but in kindness (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.7">He 12:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.8">8</reference>), and that all those things he thought against Him were working together for his good. <chapter eID="Gen.42"/>
